vsm1.10:4.5: 1. “A dog, it seems, was attacked in the forest by a boar and fled. When it was dusk he saw in the distance a cauldron for boiling rice, and perceiving it as a boar, he fled in fear and terror. Again, a man who was afraid of pisāca goblins saw a decapitated palm stump at night in a place that was unfamiliar to him, and perceiving it as a pisāca goblin, he fell down in his fear, horror and confusion” (Vism-mhṭ 320).
vsm1.10:11.2: 2. PED, this ref. reads yānapuṭosā for yānapatoḷi, taking it as one compound (see under yāna and mutoḷī, but this does not fit the context happily. Vism-mhṭ (p. 321) has: “‘Yānappatoḷikumbhimukhādīnan’ ti oguṇṭhana-sivikādi-yānaṃ mukhaṃ = yāna-mukhaṃ; patoḷiyā kuddakadvārassa mukhaṃ = patoḷi-mukhaṃ; kumbhi-mukhan ti paccekaṃ mukha- saddo sambandhitabbo.” This necessitates taking yāna separately.
vsm1.10:13.3: 3. These two quotations refer respectively to the first of the eight liberations and the first of the eight bases of mastery (See M-a III 255ff.).
vsm1.10:13.6: 4. This explanation depends on a play on the word saññā as the subjective perception and as the objective sign, signal or label perceived.
vsm1.10:14.3: 5. See XIV.129, description of perception aggregate, which is classified in the same way as the consciousness aggregate. Those referred to here are the fifteen fine-material kinds, corresponding to nos. (9–l3), (57–61) and (81–85) in Table III.
vsm1.10:16.4: 6. See XIV.96f. nos. (34–38) and (50–54) in Table III.
vsm1.10:23.1: 7. “A formed dhamma with an individual essence is delimited by rise and fall because it is produced after having not been, and because after having been it vanishes. But space is called boundless since it has neither rise nor fall because it is a dhamma without individual essence” (Vism-mhṭ 323).
